title: What patterns survive the checks?
conclusion: There are useful descriptive signals, especially a GPT-6.1 directional advantage and metric/source-shift reversals. This panel establishes no universal improvement law, no reliable causal predictor of generalist success, and no general-model victory over current strongest specialists. Failure to reject the family-level null does not show that all variation is noise.

quantitative.title: GPT-6.1 has a directional advantage on this panel, with substantial uncertainty
quantitative.text: Against GPT-6: 23 wins, seven losses and one failed comparison across 31 slices from 24 tasks in 13 families. Family-equal win fraction 0.6090; task-equal fraction 0.6875. Penalizing the newer-only failure gives signed family contrast 0.2179. Exact conditional sign-flip p=0.4463; Holm-adjusted p=1.0000. Neither significance nor no-effect is established.

quantitative.title: The version sequence is not a monotonic improvement law
quantitative.text: Among 30 slices where all three models produced numerical scores, only nine improve monotonically (allowing a numerical tie), and six of 23 complete tasks do so on every slice. GPT-6.1 is best or numerically tied-best on 20 slices but worse than both older models on five. Missing J08 is excluded from these complete-case counts. Version names do not provide compute, parameter-count or training-data measurements.

quantitative.title: Reference strata produce different apparent win rates
quantitative.status: Descriptive; confounded by task and reference selection
quantitative.text: Task-equal point-win fractions against conventional baselines are 0.7500 / 0.8333 / 0.8333 for 5.6 / 6 / 6.1 (12 tasks). Against archived specialists they are 0.3000 / 0.2500 / 0.6500 (four tasks); local specialists give 0.6000 / 0.6000 / 0.8000 (five tasks). These are different task sets, with unequal inputs and optimization histories. This is not a causal effect of specialist status, and GPT-6.1’s local-specialist rate is close to its conventional-baseline rate.

quantitative.title: Cell and molecular tasks show the most consistent multi-task category signal
quantitative.status: Retrospective category observation; hypothesis for replication
quantitative.text: GPT-6.1 beats both older versions on all four measured cell/molecular tasks: K01 morphology classification, K04 cortical-layer transfer, K05 marker-fraction calibration and K06 PV/SST waveform classification. These four are strict-format common support. This is the largest category with an all-task directional advantage for GPT-6.1 in the observed panel. It does not establish a modality law: broad source collections overlap, tasks were selected for feasibility, and K01 has a small native margin. SingleR still beats GPT-6.1 on K04 (0.5546 vs 0.5506). No category-specific significance claim is made after inspecting all categories.

qualitative.title: The tested capability is building analysis procedures
qualitative.text: All three Sol models generate numerical programs that are then fitted locally. Their wins support trying a generated algorithm baseline on a well-defined numeric endpoint. They do not establish native raw neural-data perception, general multimodal/world-model skill, autonomous experiment execution or specialist-tool-agent performance.

qualitative.title: A benchmark name does not specify the information contract
qualitative.text: Custom slices provide processed waveforms, calcium traces, pose features, expression columns, known simulator equations or small storage chunks. Supervised K05 fraction calibration differs from reference-only deconvolution; likelihood-informed L06 differs from simulator-only inference; E06 uses a subset and locally optimized NLinear. Those distinctions can explain what is feasible, but this panel cannot estimate their causal effect.

qualitative.title: Biological replication remains the main evidence gap
qualitative.text: Examples include one held-out bird in A15, two test fish in C06, one brain/session in E06 and one monkey shared by G01/B08. Many cells, frames or windows do not create independent cohorts. Most tasks have one code generation. Category resampling cannot recover missing animal, lab, generation or prompt uncertainty.

combined.title: Metric choice can reverse which model looks better
combined.status: Quantitative case evidence plus scientific interpretation
combined.text: C06 GPT-6.1 has higher correlation than GPT-5.6 (0.8676 vs 0.8564), but worse relative count error (3.2471 vs 1.9040). In B01, GPT-6 exceeds GPT-5.6 on the frozen unit metric (0.9400 vs 0.8750), but falls below it on post-hoc all-output event F1 (0.5998 vs 0.9000). Two of three B01 pairwise model orderings reverse. Calibration and extra events affect scientific use; a single primary leaderboard value cannot establish those properties.

combined.title: Within-condition improvement does not guarantee transfer
combined.status: One controlled source-shift case; hypothesis for replication
combined.text: On E06, GPT-6.1 reduces MSE versus GPT-6 by 16.6% on temporal tails, but increases it by 8.5% on the prespecified unseen-taxis slice. The same programs, training arrays, neurons and brain are used; native target distributions differ. This is a real ordering reversal, not proof of a universal transfer law or a causal mechanism.

combined.title: Failure definitions and reproducibility matter to the conclusion
combined.text: The panel has 107 numerical successes in 111 model attempts, but only 100 meet the line-format criterion as well. Two B08 failures arise from ambiguous utility-import wording and stay visible while the task is excluded from aggregate claims. J08’s GPT-6.1 numerical failure remains a loss in the conservative diagnostic. H02’s three attempts per model are separate evidence on one source, not extra independent tasks.

assumptions: Retrospective convenience panel, one program/model/task; grouped tests assume independent symmetric family contrasts. Composition intervals are not biological or generation uncertainty. No global-SOTA or scaling-law claim.
